title: As if seen
hookLine: live among people as if God saw you, speak to God as if people heard
carry: the private and public self become one

cards: Behind a closed door, where nobody will ever know, small choices get made: whether to return the extra change, whether to read the message over someone's shoulder, whether to say the unkind thing in a private chat.

The person making them isn't always the one the world sees. Seneca's tenth letter is about being alone, and it ends with a sentence that closes the gap between the two versions of a person, from both directions.

teach.h: CRATES: TALKING WITH A BAD MAN.
teach.b: It starts with a warning. Crates the Cynic saw a young man walking by himself and asked what he was doing out there alone. I'm talking with myself, the young man said.
Crates answered: be careful, then, you're talking with a bad man. Solitude is only good, Seneca says, if the company inside is good.
Then he passes on a saying of Athenodorus: you'll know you're free of your cravings when you ask God for nothing you couldn't ask for openly, in front of everyone.

Seneca notes how many people whisper prayers they'd be ashamed for others to hear. And then his own line: live among people as if God were watching; speak with God as if people were listening. Two directions.
With others, act as you would before the highest witness you know.

teach.h: ASK ONLY WHAT YOU'D ASK OPENLY.
teach.b: Alone with the highest, ask only for what you'd be glad to have heard.

teach.h: LIVE AS IF GOD SAW YOU.
teach.b: Seneca says God here. Listeners of any faith may hear that word in their own way, and those without one can think of the best witness they can imagine.
A life lived as if seen, by someone kind and clear-eyed, doesn't need two versions.
The person behind the closed door and the person in the crowd can finally be the same.

how: Some people, religious and not, try to act in private as they would before a kind and clear-eyed witness, so that their private and public lives match.

the Cynic who warned a young man alone

games.q: as if seen — tap the pairs.
p: you're talking with a bad man
ask only what you'd ask openly
live as if God were watching

s: Seneca says being alone is always good for you
only if the company inside is good; Crates warns the young man.
the open-prayer saying comes from Athenodorus
Seneca passes it on from Athenodorus.
Seneca's line only runs one way: act well in public
it runs both ways: among people as if God saw, with God as if people heard.

games.q: you're Crates. you see a young man walking alone, and he says he's talking with himself. what do you say?
o: good for you: solitude is wisdom.
careful, you're talking with a bad man.
games.why: Crates' joke has a point: solitude only helps if the company inside is good.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been wishing for privately, and imagine saying it plainly in a room full of people who know you. Notice, without judging, whether the wish changes shape when it's said in the open.
If you pray, this is Athenodorus' test; if you don't, it works on any wish.

wordCard.voice: Athenodorus. The philosopher Seneca quotes: you're free of your cravings when you ask God for nothing you couldn't ask for openly. Today's word.
